source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: A trained verifier that ranks 100 sampled solutions beats plain fine-tuning on GSM8K. The authors say the gain equals about a 30x bigger model.
numbers: GPT-3 family, 6B and 175B; verifier picks best of 100 samples; verifiers trained on 100 samples per training problem for 1 epoch.
quote: verifiers results in approximately the same performance boost as a 30x model size increase
limits: GSM8K only; final answers are checkable; verifier is trained on the same generator's samples.
agent_relevance: Baseline proof that a separate checker pays off. It is a trained checker, not the same model re-reading its own text.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: Verification does not help with small training sets. The model overfits to the correct final answer before it learns what correct reasoning looks like. It only wins once data is large enough.
numbers: Compared 6B and 175B at several training set sizes; 175B verifiers pass the fine-tune baseline with fewer problems than 6B.
limits: No exact crossover size recorded here; read from figure 5.
agent_relevance: A learned verifier needs enough labelled data. With few examples, prefer executable checks.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: More candidates help only up to a point. Accuracy rises up to 400 completions per problem for the 6B verifier, then falls, because search finds adversarial solutions that fool the verifier.
numbers: 6B verifier; peak at 400 completions per test problem, decline beyond (up to 3200 tested).
limits: Single task and model size; peak location depends on verifier quality.
agent_relevance: Cap best-of-N for any learned scorer. Budget N, do not grow it without bound (G7).

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: Token-level verifiers end up better than solution-level ones, though they train slower. A large generator with a small verifier beats a small generator with a large verifier. Voting among the top verifier-ranked answers adds a further gain.
numbers: Ablations in Fig 6a-c and 7b on GSM8K.
limits: Authors suggest the verifier may use coarse heuristics rather than real checking.
agent_relevance: Spend effort on the generator first. A cheap verifier is often enough. Combine ranking with voting in code.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Step-level (process) supervision beats outcome supervision and majority voting on hard math. The authors release PRM800K, 800K step labels.
numbers: MATH 500-problem test subset, best-of-1860: PRM 78.2%, ORM 72.4%, majority voting 69.6%. PRM800K: 800K labels, 75K solutions, 12K problems.
limits: Generator is a GPT-4 base; human labels are costly; MATH has easy-to-check final answers. Authors call the false-positive weakness of final-answer checking over-emphasized in MATH.
agent_relevance: Process checks can beat outcome checks when answers are right for wrong reasons. This is the main case for step verification.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Fair comparison matters. Outcome supervision from final-answer checking is weaker than outcome supervision labelled by the strong PRM, since the latter handles right-answer-wrong-reasoning cases. At small scale, process supervision wins at all data sizes. Active learning gives 2.6x data efficiency.
numbers: Small-scale synthetic: 1 to 200 solutions per problem, best-of-500 evaluation. Active learning: 2.6x improvement.
limits: Synthetic supervision comes from a large PRM, not humans.
agent_relevance: Gains from process checks depend on how the outcome baseline is built. Be careful to compare at equal budget.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: On fresh out-of-distribution STEM exams the PRM advantage holds but is smaller than on MATH. Majority voting ties or loses to the ORM on aggregate.
numbers: 224 recent AP and AMC problems, best-of-100, 234 scored items: ORM 63.8%, PRM 72.9%, majority 61.3%. AMC10/12 (84): ORM 49.1, PRM 53.2, majority 32.8. AP Calculus (45): 68.9, 86.7, 80.0.
limits: Small N per subject; scoring-rule choice matters little (product 78.2 vs minimum 77.6 on MATH).
agent_relevance: Learned verifiers carry over to new tasks, but the margin shrinks. Do not assume the MATH gain.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: With an automatic verifier, more samples keep solving more problems. Without one, voting and reward models stall near 100 samples while coverage keeps growing.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct 15.9% with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples, versus single-attempt state of the art 43%. CodeContests with Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples (over 300x).
limits: SWE-bench Lite and CodeContests have test-based verifiers; the authors found imperfections (see b10).
agent_relevance: Where an executable check exists, generation plus check scales. Where it does not, the check is the bottleneck.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys
finding: Large gap between coverage (oracle verifier) and what real selectors achieve on math. Majority vote and a reward model gain almost nothing from 100 to 10,000 samples.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward model: only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. Plateau around 100 samples.
limits: One policy model and one reward model family; per-problem bars show many problems where the correct answer is sampled rarely, so voting loses them.
agent_relevance: Voting cannot find a rare correct answer. A check that does not rely on frequency is needed for hard items (G4).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys
finding: Test-based verifiers are flawed. Flaky tests and test suites that reject valid alternative outputs create false negatives and positives.
numbers: 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems have flaky test suites, some rejecting the gold fix on some runs. CodeContests tests often demand one particular output when several are valid, and some mutated test inputs break the problem rules.
limits: Results with flaky problems removed were similar for SWE-bench Lite.
agent_relevance: Run execution checks more than once and allow multiple valid outputs. Treat a single test pass as evidence, not proof (G3).

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024/2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: With imperfect unit tests, a weak model cannot reach a strong model by resampling, because weak models pass the visible tests with wrong code more often. The false-positive rate rises as model capability falls.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+; at least 200 samples per task (1000 for Command Light) on HumanEval+; 50 on MBPP+. Linear inverse relation between capability and false-positive rate across Cohere Command, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 families.
limits: Coding only; hidden extended tests are assumed correct.
agent_relevance: Pass rate on given tests overstates correctness more for weak generators. G3 (a pass must be on something not fitted to) is backed.

source: Stroebl et al. (2024/2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: If false positives carry a cost, the best number of attempts is finite and low, even with free compute. False-positive rate rises with attempts K because hard tasks (bimodal difficulty) draw more false positives. False positives also have worse code quality.
numbers: Llama 3.1 70B and Code Llama 7B on HumanEval+; reward falls after small K under cost ratios tested. Readability scores lower for false positives.
limits: Cost model is stylised; matches inverse-U curves reported by Chen et al. (2024a) for voting.
agent_relevance: Set a small K for resampling against a weak check. A stricter held-out test beats more samples.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction
finding: A verifier trained to write a check and then a Yes/No answer, with majority voting over many checks (GenRM-CoT), beats discriminative reward models, DPO verifiers, LLM-as-a-judge and self-consistency in best-of-N.
numbers: GSM8K, Gemma2-9B verifier on Gemini 1.0 Pro solutions: 73% to 93.4% problems solved. Algorithmic tasks (Gemma-2B generator): 5% to 45.3%. MATH easy-to-hard: 28% to 44.6%. MMLU abstract algebra: 37.9% to 53.5%. Best-of-32 for MATH; 32 votes.
limits: Proposing authors' own framework; verifiers trained on synthetic rationales; trained on easy tasks then transferred.
agent_relevance: Written, voted checks scale with test-time compute, unlike a single score. A tested way to spend tokens on verification.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Generative Verifiers
finding: Generative verifiers scale with model size (2B, 7B, 9B) and with number of votes. Combining the verifier score with self-consistency (weighted self-consistency) beats plain voting. A discriminative RM missed an error the CoT verifier caught (score 0.999 versus 0.0015).
numbers: Gemma 2B, 7B, 9B verifiers trained on GSM8K, tested on MATH. Example case: discriminative score 0.999 on a wrong solution.
limits: Rationales can themselves be wrong, which is why votes are needed.
agent_relevance: Support for a verifier step that explains its check and is sampled several times, with code doing the aggregation.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Existing open PRMs generalise poorly to hard math and lose to prompted general models used as step critics. The top proprietary reasoning model is far ahead.
numbers: 3,400 test cases with expert error-location labels (GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH). Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K (their own) 56.5. Open critics scored with majority vote over 8 samples.
limits: Critics were scored with 8-sample majority voting; proprietary used greedy.
agent_relevance: A prompted strong model with reasoning often beats a trained step scorer. Check scorers on a step-error benchmark before use.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench
finding: PRM training labels from Monte Carlo estimates (does the step lead to a right answer) have two flaws: right answer despite a wrong step, and wrong answer despite a right step. This explains weak step-level accuracy.
numbers: PRM comparison table across four subsets; Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B and Skywork PRMs underperform prompted Qwen2.5 critics even on GSM8K and MATH.
quote: existing PRMs typically underperform the top prompt-driven critic models even on the simpler GSM8K and MATH subsets
limits: Benchmark labels from human experts on first error only.
agent_relevance: Do not label steps by whether the final answer came out right.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Monte Carlo step labels train worse PRMs than an LLM judge or human labels, when tested for finding the wrong step. The ranking flips on best-of-8, so best-of-N hides the weakness.
numbers: ProcessBench avg F1: MC Math-Shepherd 440k 28.9; MC own 860k 40.1; LLM-as-judge 860k 46.5; human PRM800K 264k 56.5. Best-of-8 avg: 64.3, 65.9, 65.3, 64.9.
limits: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct policy and PRM base; BoN differences are marginal.
agent_relevance: Judge a verifier by its error-finding accuracy, not only by best-of-N, or you will reward the wrong thing.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models
finding: Policy models often give correct final answers through flawed steps, more so on harder problems. BoN scoring only checks the answer, so PRMs that miss process errors get inflated scores.
numbers: 8 responses per query from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct on GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH; manual annotation of correct-answer responses; process-error rate grows with problem difficulty. Consensus filtering (judge and MC agree on error step) keeps about 40% of data and matches the LLM-judge model on ProcessBench.
limits: Percent per dataset is in a figure; only the trend and the 40% kept are quoted.
agent_relevance: Right answers can hide wrong reasoning. A reasoning-trace check adds information beyond answer match.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Verifier-guided search beats best-of-N at small budgets but the lead shrinks or reverses at larger budgets. Authors attribute this to exploitation of the PRM. Best-of-N does better on easy questions and at higher budgets; beam search on hard questions and low budgets.
numbers: PaLM 2 on MATH; budgets up to 256 generations; compute-optimal strategy matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute (for example 16 versus 64 generations).
limits: Needed their own PRM: a PRM trained on PRM800K was easily exploited by naive best-of-N because of distribution shift. Difficulty prediction cost not counted.
agent_relevance: Pick the verifier-search method by difficulty and budget. A verifier from another generator may not transfer.

source: Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2022) Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
finding: Pushing hard on a proxy reward makes the true (gold) reward rise then fall. Best-of-n and RL follow different functional forms. Best-of-n uses far less KL; KL for best-of-n grows about log(n).
numbers: Synthetic setup: policy 1.2B, RM data 90,000 fixed for the RM-size sweep. Fit coefficients for best-of-n change smoothly with RM size. Larger policies gain less from optimisation but do not overoptimise more.
limits: Gold RM is itself a model, not humans. Does not model mismatch between gold labels and human intent.
agent_relevance: Any learned judge is overfitted by a search. Limit N and keep an independent held-out check.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Strong LLM judges agree with human experts about as often as experts agree with each other, but with clear biases. Position bias is large, and only GPT-4 is mostly consistent.
numbers: MT-bench, no-tie setup: GPT-4 vs humans 85%, human vs human 81%. Position consistency after swapping answers: GPT-4 65.0%, Claude-v1 23.8% (it favours the first answer 75.0% of the time). Few-shot examples raise GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%.
limits: Chatbot answers, not correctness checks; humans were also biased; high consistency may not mean accuracy.
agent_relevance: Always judge in both orders and accept only agreement (the swap rule). Fits G5.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Verbosity bias: judges prefer a padded answer with no new content. Self-enhancement bias exists but evidence in this paper is weaker.
numbers: Repetitive-list attack on 23 answers: judge fooled 91.3% of the time for Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5, 8.7% for GPT-4. Self-enhancement: GPT-4 wins 10 points more often for its own answers, Claude-v1 25 points; GPT-3.5 does not favour itself.
limits: Small sample (23 answers); the authors say a controlled self-preference test is hard.
agent_relevance: Normalise length and hide authorship before any model judge (G5).

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: On math questions, judges often accept wrong answers. Having the judge solve the problem first helps little because it copies the given answer's mistake. Showing a reference answer made independently helps a lot.
numbers: 10 math questions, LLaMA-13B vs Vicuna-13B, positions swapped (20 trials): failure 14/20 default, 6/20 with chain of thought, 3/20 reference-guided. Text: failure falls from 70% to 15%.
limits: Only 20 trials; reference came from the judge's own earlier answer, so it can still be wrong.
agent_relevance: A judge needs an independent solution, not the candidate in view. Code should compare, not the model (G2, G5).

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Self-preference is linked to self-recognition. Fine-tuning a judge to recognise its own text raises how much it prefers its own text, in a linear relation.
numbers: Summarisation (CNN/DailyMail, XSUM), GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2. Out of the box GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate at telling itself from two other LLMs and humans. After 500 fine-tuning examples GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 pass 90% self-recognition. Per-example Kendall tau 0.41 for GPT-3.5 on XSUM before fine-tuning.
limits: Summaries only; causal link supported by confounder controls, not mechanism; no correctness task.
agent_relevance: Do not let the generator grade its own output, and strip style cues. G1 and G5 backed.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Earlier self-correction gains came from oracle labels telling the model when to stop. Without them, accuracy falls.
numbers: Intrinsic, GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 (rounds 1, 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K goes 75.9 to 84.3. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0 (200 questions).
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 family, 2023 era; later reasoning models trained for self-checking may differ (not tested here).
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2: revise only from real output, never from the model's opinion.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Model doubting flips right answers to wrong more often than the reverse. Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at the same number of responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K. GSM8K at equal responses: standard 76.7; self-consistency 82.5 (3), 85.3 (6), 88.2 (9); debate 83.2 (6 responses), 83.0 (9 responses).
limits: Self-consistency won here at equal count, but its limits on rare correct answers apply (b09).
agent_relevance: Count compute. Voting is a strong cheap baseline that any verifier design must beat at equal tokens (G7).

source: Synthesis of b01, b08, b09, b11 (when verification is easier than generation)
finding: Tasks with an executable or exact checker (proofs, tests, exact answers) let a weak generator plus many samples beat a single stronger try. When the checker is a learned score or a vote, gains plateau at about 100 to 400 samples and a weak model does not catch a strong one.
numbers: Executable checker: SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% with 250 samples. Learned selectors on MATH: 40.50% to 41.41% from 100 to 10,000 samples. Unit-test false positives rise as model weakens.
limits: Cross-paper synthesis; different models and tasks, so no single effect size.
agent_relevance: Route by checker quality. Exact check, use resampling. Learned or voted check, cap N small and add an independent held-out test.
